notes: [The finding most worth challenging: the gate cap pushes 87 down to 40] Un-capped, the normalised score is 85/98 = 87% (Leading band); capped, it is 40% (Early band) — a 40-byte robots.txt creating a 47-point gap. And nextjs.org's robots.txt carries no User-agent group at all — under RFC 9309 that means everything is allowed, and in testing all 80/80 retrieval-user-agent units did get the content with a 200. That is to say, the gate check that triggers the cap is not blocking any crawler in reality, and the causal claim the cap rests on ("nothing else you change has any effect until a crawler can get the content") does not hold for this site. My view is that this exposes a problem in the rubric, not in the site: g.robots tier 5 requires an explicit allow, but an explicit Allow is optional in the robots protocol and the default is to permit, so making it a capping condition amounts to penalising a compliant, minimal robots.txt. Suggested for v1.2 discussion: either change the g.robots cap so it fires only alongside a measured failure to reach the site (g.reachable dropping a tier), or make "no directive group at all" its own tier 5. I applied the cap as v1.1 literally requires, but this number should not be taken as a technical judgement of nextjs.org.

[p2.freshness, 3 or 6: I went back and forth three times] Tier 6 reads "most pages do, and dateModified agrees with the visible date". The facts: 5/8 pages carry a date; on the two documentation pages the visible "Last updated" matches the schema dateModified to the day; on the three blog posts the visible date matches dateCreated to the day but there is no dateModified; the three marketing pages carry no date at all. Read as a conjunction (a dateModified must exist and must agree), only 2/8 qualify, which scores 3; read as "most pages carry a date, and wherever a dateModified exists it does not contradict it", it scores 6. I chose 3 under rule 2, "take the highest tier the evidence actually satisfies, not the one it nearly reaches", but I am not sure that is what the rubric's author intended — given what the site actually does (all 508 documentation pages carry Last updated plus dateModified), readers may well find 3 points unfair. Changing it to 6 would make readiness 88 and the un-capped normalised score 90%; capped it is still 40, so the band does not change.

[Scoring p2.named-author 6 is the most aggressive call in this report] This check's ladder carries no per-page criterion (unlike answer-passages, which says "on most pages"), so I judged it on the quality of the byline wherever a byline exists: the 3 blog posts are 3/3 a named Person plus a resolving identity link, which is tier 6. Under a per-page reading it comes out entirely differently — only 3 of the 8 pages carry a named-person byline, and the author on the 2 documentation pages is {"@type":"Organization","name":"Vercel"}, Organization being the literal condition for tier 0; that would score 3 or even 0. That is a 6-point swing on a 6-point check. My reason for preferring 6: institutional attribution on framework documentation is industry-normal, and on the blog page type, where E-E-A-T actually bites, this site is complete (JSON-LD Person array, an on-site /team page, and four external x.com identity pages all returning 200). But I acknowledge this is an interpretation, not a measurement.

[The 9 on p2.answer-passages rests on two borderline passes] The home page's opening paragraph in the HTML is only 22 words (under the 25-word line); it passes on the strength of a 44-word blockquote in the agent-view markdown — my reasoning being that 8 of the 10 retrieval user-agents actually receive that markdown. But the rubric lays down nothing about which body to judge when one URL serves two different bodies to different user-agents; that criterion is mine. docs-install passes on a 45-word bulleted paragraph; the page's own lede is 9 words. More glaring is /learn's opening paragraph at 24 words — it fails by one word, and the v1.1 revision notes explicitly name svelte being scored 0 over a 39-word paragraph one word short as a problem to fix; the same boundary effect has now reappeared at the 25-word line. Under the strict criterion (counting only prose paragraphs in the HTML) it is 4/8, scoring 7.

[p2.sourced-stats: this ladder has no middle ground] Tier 5 is "most are attributed"; tier 7 is "most are attributed and the source is clickable and checkable". The situation on this site: 100% of the places that are attributed are clickable (direct CVE/GHSA links, a direct customer-case link, direct react.dev/nodejs.org links), but attribution coverage is only about 29% (I counted roughly 35 numbers and factual claims, of which roughly 10 carry a source). That collapses the judgement into a binary — reach "most" and it is 7 points outright, fall short and it is 3, and tier 5 is in practice unreachable given this site's structure. Between 3 and 7 there is a 4-point jump, and my 29% denominator was counted by hand: whether blog-turbo's three-column benchmark table counts as 1 item or 15 could flip the conclusion. This counting criterion should be pinned down in v1.2.

[Two tier descriptions do not match the facts; I took the tier by score, but the wording is wrong] First, p1.organization scores 3, whose tier description is "one of the two present", yet on this site the Organization and WebSite nodes are both in the same @graph, cross-referenced by @id, and Organization carries a further 4 sameAs entries — all it lacks is a logo property (grep "logo" across the 16 sampled responses site-wide: 0 matches). Because logo sits at tier 5 and sameAs at tier 6, a site that has sameAs but no logo is pushed back to the same score as a site with only one entity. Second, p3.video scores 2, whose tier description is "a channel exists but content is sparse", whereas the reality is a Vercel channel with 474 videos and 116K subscribers carrying every Next.js Conf session — not sparse in the slightest; it is held below tier 3 only because VideoObject on the site is 0 (and the 25 /conf session pages carry not even an ld+json block). In both cases I suggest splitting the conjunctive conditions and re-ordering the rungs.

[Scoring g.reachable 5 is a discretionary call putting substance ahead of the letter] One of tier 3's conditions is that the body differs from what a browser receives, and this site returns text/markdown to 8 retrieval user-agents and text/html to browsers, differing in bytes and in MD5 — a literal tier-3 match. My basis for scoring 5 is v1.1 rule 6, "substance over format": the difference is an upgrade for AI retrieval that the site declares publicly (llms.txt states "Recognised agents get markdown there automatically"), and the markdown holds the same body text plus structured front-matter metadata of title/url/lastUpdated/prerequisites — it is neither cloaking nor degradation. I have also verified character by character that where the size matches but the MD5 differs (for example /learn's 411339 bytes), the difference is a per-request random React key, not content. To be clear, this call does not affect the report's conclusion — g.robots has already triggered the cap, so 3 or 5 here changes neither gate_capped nor the final 40; it only changes the un-capped 87% and the readiness of 85. But on another site it could be decisive, so it is recorded here.

[Sampling representativeness is skewed, and systematically against this site] 3 of the 8 sampled pages (the home page, /learn, /showcase) are marketing/index pages — 37.5% of the sample, but 3 of the sitemap's 734 URLs (0.4%). Those 3 pages happen to be exactly the ones with no date, no lists or tables, no byline, no self-contained answer passage and no page-type schema, which directly depressed three checks: freshness, answer-passages and question-intent. Conversely /docs, which is 69% of the site (508 URLs), contributed only 2 pages to the sample. The fixed ratio in rubric rule 1 (1 homepage + 2 product pages + 2 documentation pages + 3 content pages) distorts an open-source site whose content is 95% documentation — it samples a documentation site as if it were a commercial one. This audit cannot fix that, but readers re-checking the work should know: a different, equally compliant sample (two more documentation pages, say) would give different scores on several checks.

citation.note: Not measured. AI citation performance is an outcome metric; under v1.1 it is reported separately from site readiness and is never folded into the main score. The scope of this engagement was a readiness audit of what is observable from outside the site, and no real industry questions were run against engines such as ChatGPT / Perplexity / Google AI Overviews / Claude. Three substantive reasons for not measuring it: (1) the same question asked repeatedly returns different results, so a single measurement is not reproducible, and putting it in the report would hand the client a number that no longer holds next week; (2) it is produced by readiness plus time, and everything the site owner can fix now is already covered by the 20 scored checks above; (3) there is no re-checkable measurement record from this engagement (no conversation screenshots, no timestamps, no question list), and under rule 8, "a judgement with no evidence does not stand", leaving it blank is better than publishing a guess. If it is to be measured later, the suggested method: fix 10 questions that front-end developers genuinely ask (the same 10 used for p4.question-coverage), ask each of them 3 times on each of 4 engines, record how many times nextjs.org is cited and which URLs are cited, and present that as a separate table annotated with the measurement time window. One prior judgement about this metric, added here (not scored, not carried into the conclusions): on the technical preconditions for being cited, this site does more than sites typically do — a 3970025-byte full-text aggregate at /docs/llms-full.txt, deliberate text/markdown content negotiation for 8 retrieval user-agents, a /.well-known/ai-catalog.json resource catalogue, and rel=alternate type=text/markdown in the head — but whether that converts into a higher citation rate can only be measured, not inferred.
